title: Short Stuff: Johnny Ringo
summary: Short Stuff episode on Old West gunslinger Johnny Ringo. Covers his birth in Greens Fork, Indiana, and the 1850s wagon-train incident in which his father Martin Ringo died from an accidental shotgun or rifle discharge. After moving to Mason County, Texas, in 1870, he fell in with former Texas Ranger Scott Cooley and got caught up in the Mason County War (Hoodoo War) starting in 1875, including the killing of deputy John Worley. Ringo later took part in violent acts across New Mexico, Arizona and Texas, was linked to the Earp and Doc Holliday circle in Tombstone (including the Tombstone movie portrayal), and was found dead near a tree outside Tombstone on July 14, 1882 with a gunshot wound to the head. Suicide is the leading explanation, with the Holliday-killing theory discussed and largely discounted, citing Kate Cummings' sympathetic written account.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Old West gunslinger Johnny Ringo as the episode topic, joking about draw and song references.

segments.title: Ringo's background and father's death
segments.summary: Ringo was born in May 1850 in what is now Greens Fork, Indiana. On a wagon train from Missouri to California, his father Martin Ringo died when a rifle or shotgun went off near his head, in front of Johnny.

segments.title: Move to San Jose and Texas
segments.summary: After the family settled in San Jose, Ringo moved to Mason County, Texas, around 1870 and fell in with a gang of cattle rustlers. He met former Texas Ranger turned outlaw Scott Cooley.

segments.title: Mason County feud and the Hoodoo War
segments.summary: Mason County had feuds between German and British-descended cattle ranchers. In 1875 Brits Tim Williamson and others were taken from jail and killed by Germans. Cooley blamed deputy John Worley, who was killed and scalped on August 10, 1875, starting the Mason County War, also called the Hoodoo War.

segments.title: Transition break
segments.summary: Hosts pause before returning to the story.

segments.title: Ringo's role in the Hoodoo War
segments.summary: Ringo supported Cooley in the war. After Moses Baird was killed, in September 1875 Ringo shot two suspected of the murder, Dave Dool and James Cheney. He was jailed but escaped.

segments.title: Ringo's outlaw years and the Tombstone connection
segments.summary: Ringo moved through New Mexico, Arizona and Texas, committing violent acts including a pistol whipping and shooting, a murder of a man harassing a woman, and robbing a poker game. He had feuds with Doc Holliday and Wyatt Earp, and his fame was linked to them, including portrayal in the movie Tombstone.

segments.title: Tombstone showdown and idioms
segments.summary: Ringo had a near showdown with Holliday and the Earps in Tombstone, broken up by a local constable. The hosts discuss the phrase 'I'm your huckleberry' from the film.

segments.title: Ringo's death and suicide theory
segments.summary: Ringo was found dead near a tree outside Tombstone on July 14, 1882, with a single gunshot wound to the head and a revolver in hand. He had been drinking, was depressed, and had told the Tombstone Epitaph he expected to be killed. Historian Bob Boss Bell and others consider suicide most likely.

segments.title: Doc Holliday murder theory
segments.summary: Whispers held that Holliday or Earp associates killed Ringo, and the 1993 movie popularized this. The hosts note Holliday was in Colorado in court at the time, and Wyatt Earp claimed credit, though that claim is doubtful.

segments.title: Account of Kate Cummings
segments.summary: Doc Holliday's common-law wife Kate Cummings wrote a sympathetic description of Ringo as handsome, gentlemanly and sad, with something in his life only he knew about, supporting the view of a tragic figure.

segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: Hosts conclude Ringo was an unsung outlaw and sign off as Short Stuff ends.
